stimulus.source_note: Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900, public domain.
stimulus.text: "I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific. … But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines. … It should, it seems to me, be our pleasure and duty to make these people free, and let them deal with their own domestic questions in their own way. And so I am an anti-imperialist. I am opposed to having the eagle put its talons on any other land." — Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900, public domain.
stem: Twain says he changed his mind because he came to believe that American rule in the Philippines meant

options.text: Too little profit for American businesses
options.misconception: Twain never mentions profit. His objection is about freedom, not about money.
No European navy appears in the passage. Twain's worry is what America would do to Filipinos.

options.text: A violation of the Open Door policy in China
options.misconception: Background: the Open Door is about trade in China. Twain's subject is the Philippines, not China.

rationales.A: Twain's own words give the reason: "we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines."
rationales.B: Twain never mentions profit. His objection is about freedom, not about money.
rationales.C: No European navy appears in the passage. Twain's worry is what America would do to Filipinos.
rationales.D: The Open Door is about trade in China. Twain's subject is the Philippines, not China.
rationales.general:
1. Find the turning point. "But I have thought some more, since then" marks the change.
2. Read the sentence after it. America does not intend to free Filipinos, but to subjugate them.
3. Check the other options. Profit, navies, and China trade never appear in the passage.
4. Put it together. The word "subjugate" is the whole reason: liberation was the promise, subjugation is the reality he sees.
Remember: the sentence right after "but" usually carries the writer's real reason.
